title: “It looks like another low BP”
note: Fictional patient. Doses and energies are quoted from the 2025 AHA guidelines (and the ERC where named) for recognition; your unit protocol, crash-cart stock and the attending nephrologist come first. Simulation success is an educational result, not a prediction of patient survival.
intro: Mr. Danilo Reyes, 59, often has low pressure in his last hour of dialysis in Davao City. The pressure alarm sounds. He is slumped, eyes half open, with a snoring breath every few seconds. A colleague says, “Another low BP. Legs up, saline bolus?”

choices.text: Breathing and a definite pulse together, within 10 seconds.
choices.feedback: Slumped and snoring every few seconds may be agonal breathing. Breathing and pulse separate arrest from hypotension.

choices.text: Give a saline bolus through the circuit first, since late-session collapse is almost always low pressure.
choices.feedback: Treating the pressure first can waste the critical minute of an arrest.
choices.then: As the saline runs, you check: no definite pulse.

choices.text: Look at the monitor: the rhythm is regular and organized, so he has a circulation and is likely fainting.
choices.feedback: A regular rhythm on the monitor cannot prove a pulse.
choices.then: You feel the neck anyway: no pulse.

n2.scene: No definite pulse. The snoring breaths are irregular gasps. The monitor still shows a regular narrow rhythm at 64.
n2.prompt: What is this, and what do you say?

choices.text: “Not breathing normally, no pulse: code! Chair flat, compressions.”
choices.feedback: Gasping without a pulse is cardiac arrest; organized rhythm without a pulse is PEA. This is pulseless electrical activity (PEA).

choices.text: Respiratory arrest: open the airway and give rescue breaths only, since the monitor still shows a rhythm.
choices.feedback: There is no pulse, so this is cardiac arrest. Breaths alone do not circulate blood.
choices.then: A second nurse confirms no pulse and starts compressions.

choices.text: Recheck the blood pressure cuff and the leads first; a slipped cuff often reads as no pressure.
choices.feedback: A cuff reading does not change a pulseless patient’s algorithm.

n3.scene: Compressions are running. The circuit nurse has stopped fluid removal. There is no air, no abnormal blood color, and the lines are intact.
n3.prompt: Which causes do you raise for this late-session PEA?

choices.text: Hypovolemia from fluid removal, bleeding at the access, low potassium or calcium from the bath.
choices.feedback: Late-session arrest points to volume and falling electrolytes; PEA is treated by finding the cause. Lift the blanket to check the access, then work through the rest; saline through the circuit per protocol.

choices.text: High potassium first, as in every dialysis arrest, so calcium and bicarbonate before anything else.
choices.feedback: Potassium is always on the list, but late in the session volume and low electrolytes are more likely.
choices.then: The leader adds volume and the access check.

choices.text: None in particular: give the arrest drugs on time and wait for the physician to look for a cause.
choices.feedback: In PEA the cause is often the only way back.
choices.then: You lift the blanket: the access is dry. You give saline per protocol.

n4.scene: After epinephrine and saline through the circuit, the next rhythm check shows a narrow rhythm at 98 with a palpable pulse; pressure 88/52.

choices.text: ROSC: pads on, oxygen, pressure support per physician, ECG, call the attending; no restart.
choices.feedback: ROSC is a pulse and a pressure. Dialysis restarts only on the attending’s decision. Check glucose and potassium and arrange transfer; dialysis is not restarted.

choices.text: Reconnect and finish the last 40 minutes of dialysis, so the potassium and fluid targets for today are still met.
choices.feedback: Restarting a circuit in an unstable patient after arrest risks re-arrest and is the attending’s decision.
choices.then: The physician-on-duty stops the restart and calls the attending.

end.title: 3:50 p.m.
end.text: Mr. Reyes leaves by ambulance with a pulse. The debrief records one habit: in every slumped patient, breathing and pulse come before blood pressure.

debrief:
What this case teaches

  • Breathing and pulse first. A familiar pattern (“another low BP”) can hide an arrest.
  • The rhythm does not prove a pulse. Regular narrow rhythm without a pulse is PEA.
  • Late-session arrest: volume, the access, and low electrolytes lead the cause list.
